source: Occupational Therapy for Children and Adolescents (Case-Smith & O'Brien, 8th Edition)
content:
Cerebral Palsy (CP) is a non-progressive permanent disorder of posture and movement caused by damage to the immature brain.
Classification:
1. GMFCS (Gross Motor Function Classification System): Level I (Walks without restrictions), Level II (Walks with limitations), Level III (Walks using a hand-held mobility device), Level IV (Self-mobility with limitations; powered mobility), Level V (Transported in a manual wheelchair; severe head/trunk limitations).
2. MACS (Manual Ability Classification System): Levels I to V categorizing how children handle everyday objects in daily activities.
OT Principles & Interventions:
- Postural Control & Seating: 90-90-90 hip-knee-ankle positioning with neutral pelvic tilt, lateral trunk supports, and pommel to prevent adductor scissoring.
- Neurodevelopmental Treatment (NDT - Bobath): Key points of control (proximal: pelvis, shoulder girdle; distal: hands, feet) to inhibit abnormal reflex patterns (ATNR, STNR, TLR) and facilitate righting and equilibrium reactions.
- Hand Function & Upper Extremity: Weight-bearing through extended wrist/open palm to break flexor hypertonicity; thumb abduction splints to facilitate radial palmar grasp; bilateral play activities.
- Assistive Feeding: Adaptive spoons with built-up angled handles, dycem non-slip mats, cut-out cups (nose cut-out) to avoid neck hyperextension during swallowing.

source: Occupational Therapy for Children and Adolescents (Case-Smith & O'Brien, 8th Edition)
content:
Ayres Sensory Integration (ASI) theory proposes that sensory processing difficulties interfere with functional participation and adaptive responses.
Sensory Systems:
1. Proprioceptive System: Muscle spindle and joint receptor inputs; provides calming, organizing effect on the central nervous system. Interventions: 'Heavy work' (carrying weighted balls, pushing therapy balls, wall push-ups, crawling through obstacle courses).
2. Vestibular System: Inner ear apparatus (semicircular canals and otolith organs) detecting head movement and gravity. Linear acceleration (hammock/glider swinging) promotes calming and organizing; rotary/angular movement is highly stimulating and alerting.
3. Tactile System: Protective (anterolateral) vs Discriminative (dorsal column) pathways. Tactile Defensiveness: Negative emotional or behavioral reaction to light touch sensations. Management: Deep pressure, proprioceptive input, Wilbarger Brushing Protocol (surgical brush deep pressure strokes followed by joint compressions).
Sensory Diet: A personalized, scheduled daily menu of sensory activities designed to keep the child in an optimal alert state for learning, social engagement, and ADLs.

source: Occupational Therapy for Children and Adolescents (Case-Smith & O'Brien, 8th Edition)
content:
Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and ADHD Interventions in OT:
1. Structured Teaching (TEACCH): Physical organization of therapy room (distinct activity zones), visual schedules, first-then boards, work-station trays with clear start/finish criteria.
2. Social Stories (Carol Gray): Descriptive, perspective, directive, and affirmative sentences preparing the child for challenging transitions or sensory environments (haircuts, dentist, school cafeteria).
3. ADHD & Sensory Motor Accommodations: Move-n-sit dynamic cushions, weighted lap pads, wobble chairs, therapy ball seating, scheduled sensory motor movement breaks (5-minute heavy work circuit).
4. Handwriting Interventions: Pencil grasp progression (palmar supinate -> digital pronate -> static quadrupod -> dynamic tripod grasp). Evaluation with Beery VMI (Visual-Motor Integration), handwriting slant boards, pencil grips, and multi-sensory letter formation (sand trays, Wikki Stix, shaving cream).
